# Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD — facts

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The authors of the original case-control study hypothesize that isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is a prodromal phenotype for the body-first type, and a later longitudinal study states that the presence of rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) may be indicative of a body-first pattern. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11150376/
- [statement] The commentary states that post hoc confounder analysis showed inclusion of indeterminate participants would not substantially change the study's main findings, while the exclusion of about one-quarter of the initial study population may limit the clinical applicability and generalizability of the subtyping criteria. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7821233/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- [statement] Applying a pragmatic approach based on motor asymmetry, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, and orthostatic hypotension to a large cohort of persons with early PD (disease duration <5 years), the authors report that individuals classified as probable brain-first were more often tremor-dominant and showed a trend toward less constipation after adjusting for disease duration, age and sex. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13746290/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- [statement] One meta-analysis reports that differences in microbiome structure between PD and controls are small, and a later meta-analysis states that causality cannot be established from predominantly observational studies. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00156-z · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13642692/
- [statement] Two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled fecal microbiota transplantation trials in Parkinson's disease report different primary-outcome results, and they differ in delivery route, comparator and primary-outcome time point: the trial at 4 hospitals in Finland (FMT or placebo via colonoscopy; primary end point at 6 months) reports that the primary outcome did not differ between the groups, whereas GUT-PARFECT (nasojejunal FMT with healthy donor stool or the participant's own stool; primary outcome at 12 months) reports that the MDS-UPDRS motor score improved by a mean of 5.8 points in the healthy donor group and by 2.7 points in the placebo group (p = 0.0235). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11287445/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11056595/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] In the brain-first versus body-first model, brain-first Parkinson's disease has α-synuclein pathology initially arising in the brain and spreading to the peripheral autonomic nervous system, while body-first Parkinson's disease has pathology originating in the enteric or peripheral autonomic nervous system and then spreading to the brain. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11150376/
- [statement] In the case-control PET study, the authors report that RBD-positive Parkinson's disease patients and iRBD patients showed reduced mean MIBG heart:mediastinum ratios and reduced colon donepezil standard uptake values compared with RBD-negative patients, and a scientific commentary in the same journal describes the reduced gut cholinergic and cardiac noradrenergic ligand binding in both groups as major support for the body-first disease subtype. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32830221/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7821233/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] In their own review, the authors who proposed the model report that molecular imaging studies were generally in agreement with the model, whereas structural imaging studies, such as MRI volumetry, showed conflicting findings. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38519273/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- [statement] In a longitudinal analysis using possible premotor RBD as the proxy for the body-first subtype, the authors report a lower MDS UPDRS-III score at baseline (p = 0.022) but a faster progression rate (p = 0.009) than in patients without possible RBD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11150376/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- [statement] Two meta-analyses of PD gut microbiome studies report depletion of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium and Lachnospiraceae, and enrichment of Akkermansia. (medium confidence) — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41531-021-00156-z · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13642692/
- [statement] In limited phenotype-stratified subgroup analyses, the authors report that gut-first PD phenotypes showed potentially more pronounced dysbiosis patterns than brain-first phenotypes, a preliminary observation based on very few phenotype-stratified studies that requires validation in larger, prospective cohorts. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13642692/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
- [statement] The GUT-PARFECT paper title describes a phase 2 trial, whereas the registry record NCT03808389 lists phase NA, with the record status verified 2023-01. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2024-03-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11056595/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD · also: https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT03808389
- [statement] In a preprint of an autopsy study of 50 PD subjects, the authors report that a positive SAA or IHC result was restricted to the GI tract in only 2 subjects while Lewy body pathology by either SAA or IHC was restricted to the brain in 11 subjects. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13042094/ · keywords: Gut-brain axis: microbiome and body-first versus brain-first PD
